# Worth Your Time

The recommendation is an editorial judgment. Every link has to earn the reader's attention.

## Purpose

Worth Your Time recommends work that an editor or contributor has fully
evaluated. Each note identifies the likely reader, the time or setup required,
the specific value of the item, its limits, and any relationship to its
creator.

## Reader expectation

Readers should be able to trust that an editor or contributor has read, watched, listened to, or tested the item being recommended. Each note should tell them:

- what the item is;
- what makes it worth their time;
- who will get the most from it;
- how much time or effort it asks;
- any access requirement, paywall, conflict, or meaningful limitation.

A reader should know enough to make an informed choice without having the item's entire argument spoiled.

## What belongs

- Articles with original reporting, a strong argument, unusual access, or lasting explanatory value.
- Podcast episodes that reward the time required to hear them.
- Videos whose visual form adds understanding.
- GitHub projects with clear utility, craft, or instructive code.
- Research papers with an important finding or method.
- Social posts that contain firsthand evidence, expert explanation, or an idea worth preserving beyond the feed.
- Tools that have been tested and solve a real problem.
- Older work that has become newly relevant or has retained unusual value.

The source may be famous or obscure. Selection depends on the quality of the work and the usefulness of the recommendation.

## What does not

- Link dumps.
- Items selected because they are trending.
- Work the recommender has only skimmed.
- Generic summaries that give no reason to follow the link.
- Promotional material presented without disclosure.
- A social post that merely repeats a claim from an unlinked source.
- A tool recommended from its feature list without testing.
- Several near-identical links included to make a list feel complete.

## Typical length

An individual recommendation usually needs 100 to 250 words. A curated edition usually contains four to eight items and runs from 700 to 1,600 words.

The count should remain small enough that every item feels chosen. One excellent recommendation is a complete edition when one is all the editor can defend.

## Tone

Give a specific reason to choose each item. The note should sound like an
informed friend who knows the reader still gets to decide.

Enthusiasm needs evidence. Explain any limitation that affects the
recommendation, and cut promotional superlatives, forced intimacy, and vague
praise.

## Publishing philosophy

The recommender must consume the full item whenever its form permits and test
tools under ordinary conditions. Follow citations when a factual claim is
central. Credit the creator, use the most direct stable link, and disclose any
relevant relationship.

Commentary should help the reader choose while leaving the original worth
visiting.

## Success metric

The section succeeds when readers consistently find work they are glad they chose and can explain why the recommendation fit them. Useful signals include:

- readers saving or returning to an edition;
- readers following a recommendation and reporting that it delivered on the note;
- low rates of dead links, undisclosed access barriers, and mischaracterized work;
- a healthy range of sources, formats, subjects, and creators over time;
- periodic editorial checks confirming that recommended tools still work and evergreen links still lead to the intended source.

Outbound clicks show that a note prompted action. They do not show whether the time was well spent, so they should be read alongside direct reader response and editorial review.

## Internal examples

- A forty-minute interview contains a working designer's account of a practice
  rarely documented elsewhere. Point readers to the useful segment and name
  the time commitment.
- An open-source tool makes a cumbersome research task repeatable. State the
  conditions in which the test worked and the setup it required.
- A paper changes an editor's view of online communities. Give the central
  insight and the limitation that makes the full method worth reading.
- A years-old essay clarifies a current cultural argument better than the
  week's commentary. Explain why it has become useful again.

## Anti-examples

- "Five things we loved this week" followed by one sentence per link.
- A podcast recommendation based on the guest's reputation.
- A tool praised with language copied from its landing page.
- A paper described only through its abstract.
- A thread included because it received a large number of likes.
- A sponsor, friend's project, or staff member's work recommended without disclosure.
- A note so complete that the reader has no reason to visit the original work.
